short: A read of the published DOJ AI use case inventory: what is deployed, what is high-impact, which vendors, and the state of the required safeguards.
title: The DOJ AI Use Case Inventory
subtitle: 314 systems, 114 high-impact, and what the risk columns say
body_html:
On this page

  • The finding
  • What the inventory is
  • What DOJ is running
  • The safeguards columns
  • How to read this fairly
  • What it means if you sell to government
  • Method
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

The Department of Justice 2025 AI use case inventory lists 314 AI systems, and DOJ itself marks 114 of them high-impact. OMB Memorandum M-25-21 requires seven minimum risk-management practices for high-impact AI: pre-deployment testing, an AI impact assessment, independent review, ongoing monitoring, periodic training, a fail-safe, and an appeal process. Across all 114 high-impact systems, the inventory records not a single one of those seven as complete. 73 report every practice as in progress. The other 41 report nothing in those columns at all.

The finding

The form offered other answers. Each of those columns has a yes option, and a separate option for a practice the agency’s Chief AI Officer has waived and reported to OMB. Neither is used for any high-impact system.

What the inventory is

Every federal agency must maintain an inventory of its AI use cases under OMB Memorandum M-25-21 and the Advancing American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2022, submit it to OMB, and publish a public version. DOJ publishes its as a spreadsheet, and the spreadsheet is the point: it carries structured answers rather than prose, which means it can be counted.

DOJ describes its own method in the file. Component representatives from its Emerging Technology Board and AI governance working groups worked with the DOJ Chief AI Officer to consolidate submissions. Similar widely adopted tools were merged into single department-wide entries, which is why the use case IDs are not sequential. DOJ says it applied the FOIA standard when deciding what to release and erred toward partial release rather than full withholding.

That last decision is visible in the data. Of 314 use cases, none is marked as withheld from public reporting. Whatever else this inventory shows, it is not an agency hiding.

What DOJ is running

314 use cases. 163 deployed, 107 pre-deployment, 25 in pilot, 19 retired from the prior year.

By component

FBI 50, DEA 43, ATF 34, Federal Bureau of Prisons 32, US Marshals Service 19, Civil Division 17, Tax Division 14, Antitrust Division 10, department-wide 10, OCDETF 10, Office of the Inspector General 9, Executive Office for United States Attorneys 8, and a long tail.

By purpose

Law enforcement 170, administrative functions 62, information technology 34, health and medical 7, procurement and financial management 6, service delivery 5, human resources 4, cybersecurity 3.

Bought, not built

153 purchased from a vendor, 21 developed with both contracting and in-house resources, 14 developed in-house. Named vendors across the file include Microsoft, Thomson Reuters, Axon, Veritone, SAS, Adobe, LexisNexis and Palantir. High-impact entries name systems including Palantir, ShotSpotter, Axon FUSUS, Cell Hawk, LexisNexis Babel Street, Spokeo, Thomson Reuters CLEAR and Dun & Bradstreet business data, several accessed through state or local partners rather than held by DOJ directly.

Personal data and authorisation

152 use cases involve personally identifiable information. 85 have an Authorization to Operate; 103 record that they do not.

The safeguards columns

DOJ marks 114 systems high-impact. A further 32 were presumed high-impact and then determined not to be, and 168 are not high-impact. The high-impact label matters because it is what triggers the seven practices in the table above.

The 73 and 41 split is worth naming precisely. 73 systems carry a consistent in-progress answer across all seven columns, which reads as a department-wide position rather than seven separate judgements. The remaining 41 leave those columns empty. An empty cell is not a claim that a practice is absent. It is an absence of any claim, which for a published transparency artifact is its own kind of answer.

How to read this fairly

Three caveats belong on this page, and they cut in DOJ’s favour.

The inventory is a snapshot, and the file carries no publication date. Practices recorded as in progress may have completed since. This page reports what the published file says, not what is true today.

In progress is not non-compliance. M-25-21 issued on April 3, 2025. The HHS compliance plan states that the deadline for applying minimum risk management practices to high-impact AI is April 3, 2026, and that tools not meeting it stop. An inventory compiled during that year showing work underway is what a year of work underway looks like.

DOJ published this voluntarily and in full. An agency that wanted this to look better had a compliant way to do it: withhold entries under a FOIA exemption, or mark fewer systems high-impact. DOJ did neither. The reason anyone can count these numbers is that DOJ chose to publish them.

The honest summary is not that DOJ is failing. It is that the largest published high-impact AI estate in the federal government reached the year mark with none of the required safeguards recorded as finished, and that the deadline after which non-compliant tools are meant to stop has now passed.

What it means if you sell to government

Every one of those 114 high-impact systems needs evidence attached to it, and 153 of the 314 were bought rather than built. The agency cannot produce pre-deployment testing evidence for a vendor product on its own. It has to ask you.

Three things follow. A vendor that can hand a customer a testing record, a monitoring approach and a documented fail-safe is solving the agency’s deadline problem rather than adding to it. A vendor that cannot is a candidate for the stop. And a product accessed through a state or local partner, as several of these are, still lands in a federal inventory, so being one step removed from the contract does not put you outside the question.

Method

Counts on this page were taken directly from the published workbook, sheet Reportable AI Use Cases, by reading the structured answer columns rather than the prose fields. High-impact means the entry recorded as high-impact, excluding the separate presumed-then-determined-not category. The seven safeguards are the columns for pre-deployment testing, AI impact assessment, independent review, ongoing monitoring, periodic training, fail-safe and appeal process. No figure on this page is estimated or inferred.

Primary sources

  • Department of Justice, 2025 AI Use Case Inventory, published workbook, sheet Reportable AI Use Cases.
  • OMB Memorandum M-25-21, Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust, April 3, 2025.
  • HHS, Compliance Plan for OMB Memorandum M-25-21, September 30, 2025, for the April 3, 2026 deadline.
  • DOJ Privacy Impact Assessments, linked from the inventory for associated use cases.

meta_description: The Justice Department published 314 AI use cases. It marks 114 high-impact. Against the seven safeguards OMB M-25-21 requires, none is recorded as complete.
